title: Colts May Sit Jonathan Taylor If Trade Talks Continue, NBC Sports Reports
body:
The Indianapolis Colts’ front office has signaled that the franchise’s rebuilding engine is still humming, and the latest buzz centers on running back Jonathan Taylor. According to league insiders, if the former Ohio State star becomes available in a trade, Indianapolis could elect to sit him out of the upcoming Sunday matchup while negotiations unfold. The move would underscore a broader strategy that has already reshaped the roster, highlighted by Tuesday’s high‑profile deals that shipped Pro Bowl left tackle Quenton Nelson to Seattle and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to San Francisco.

The two blockbuster trades marked the most aggressive roster turnover the Colts have seen in years. Nelson, a five‑time All‑Pro who anchored the offensive line for a decade, was exchanged for a package that includes a 2025 second‑round pick, a 2026 fourth‑rounder and a veteran defensive end. Buckner, a former first‑team All‑Pro who helped anchor the “No Fly Zone” during the team’s 2020 run, headed to the 49ers for a 2024 third‑round selection and a future seventh‑rounder. Both moves reflect a clear pivot toward accumulating draft capital and shedding salary commitments, a shift that aligns with the organization’s long‑term timeline under new general manager Chris Ballard.

If Taylor does indeed become a trade chip, the Colts’ decision to bench him for the upcoming game would be a calculated risk. Taylor, who rushed for 1,300 yards and 12 touchdowns last season, remains the most valuable asset on the roster. Sitting him could preserve his health and protect his market value, especially if the team hopes to command a premium return. Moreover, the Colts have already demonstrated a willingness to prioritize future flexibility over short‑term production, a philosophy that could see them field a more experimental lineup on Sunday while scouting potential suitors.

The trade speculation also raises questions about Indianapolis’s offensive identity moving forward. Without Nelson’s elite pass‑protection, the line will rely heavily on younger players like Wyatt Teller and newly acquired free‑agent guards to keep the backfield clean. If Taylor were to depart, the Colts would likely lean on a committee approach, featuring backup backs such as Nyheim Hines and a possible increased role for rookie running back Jaxon Smith‑Neri. This could force head coach Shane Steichen to lean more on play‑action and the passing game, potentially accelerating the development of quarterback Anthony Richardson, who is still finding his footing in the NFL.

From a league‑wide perspective, the possibility of a Jonathan Taylor trade would reverberate through the AFC North and beyond. Teams in need of a proven bell‑cow—such as the Pittsburgh Steelers, who have struggled to replace Ben Roethlisberger’s production, or the Buffalo Bills, who could use a power runner to complement Josh Allen’s dual‑threat skill set—might be willing to part with significant draft capital. Conversely, the Colts could leverage Taylor’s name recognition to acquire multiple picks, bolstering their already deep pool of young talent and giving Ballard more ammunition to continue the roster overhaul.

Looking ahead, the Colts’ next moves will likely be defined by how quickly they can translate their draft haul into on‑field impact. If the trade talks materialize and Taylor departs, Indianapolis could emerge with a refreshed core of high‑upside prospects ready to take the field in 2025. Even if the running back remains, the organization’s willingness to entertain a benching underscores a pragmatic, business‑first approach that could set the tone for the remainder of the season. As the Sunday game approaches, fans and analysts alike will be watching not just the final score, but the strategic calculus that could reshape the Colts’ trajectory for years to come.
